rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3-4 report the authors' own Tetis hydrological model runs (240 simulations) for the Valencia study area. Q2: Section 3.2.3 states the model was calibrated against observed ETa in flood and drip sectors, monthly groundwater levels in four wells and plot-scale soil moisture (12 behavioural parameterizations); Section 4.3.2 and Figure 8 report control-period mean monthly recharge of 14.3 mm under drip vs 19.1 mm under flood; Section 4.4 reports annual recharge of 169-175 mm (drip) vs 233-248 mm (flood); Conclusion 2 states recharge is higher in flood than drip irrigation. Q4: Sections 3.2.1 and 4.2 describe the modelled soil water storages, irrigation volumes (about 630 vs 490 mm/yr, Figure 4 bars), wetted fraction (53%) and rooting depth that generate recharge, and show recharge peaks in flood irrigation coinciding with irrigation turns. Q6: Section 2 and Figure 1 describe a 913 km2 study area with 68 irrigation sectors (419 km2); results are aggregated at irrigation-sector and regional scale (Figures 8-9). Q8: Section 5.3 lists limitations: farmer behaviour (cropping, pumping) not considered, constant irrigation schedules, no vegetation/CO2 feedback, static FAO crop coefficients. Q9: Figures 3-5 and 8 report the range across five climate models and boxplots of 60 values (12 parameterizations x 5 GCM-RCMs) for recharge under drip and flood.
rows.notes: Single-method modelling study (one hydrological model), so no triangulation. One region, one dominant crop (citrus), loam/clay-loam soils, so not representative across sites. The study shows lower simulated recharge under drip but does not report groundwater levels or return flows directly as the passage asserts. The business-as-usual irrigation schedule is a modelling assumption rather than a stated requirement, so Q7 is no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3-4 report the authors' own model chain (2 RCPs, 5 GCM-RCMs, 12 parameterizations, 2 irrigation scenarios). Q2: Section 3.2.3 reports calibration of the model against observed ETa, groundwater levels and soil moisture in the study area; Section 4.3.1.1 and Figure 5 report statistically significant recharge reductions only under RCP 8.5, more pronounced in drip (-6.6% near-term, -9.3% mid-term) than flood (-2.4%, -7.3%); Section 4.4 reports that the planned transformation to drip enhances the negative recharge trend to 5.1-7.0 mm/yr. Q4: Sections 4.3.1.1 and 4.2 model the intermediate drivers, showing recharge trends follow projected precipitation decreases (-6.5% to -6.6% mid-term) and simulated ETa and soil water storage under each technique. Q6: Results are reported for the 913 km2 region and 68 irrigation sectors (Figures 1, 9), i.e., district/regional scale. Q8: Section 5.2 discusses uncertainty in magnitude and sign of change; Section 5.3 lists limitations: farmer behaviour not included, constant irrigation schedule, no vegetation/CO2 feedback, static crop coefficients. Q9: Figures 3-7 report the range across five climate models and boxplots of 60 ensemble values per scenario; Section 5.2 notes the GCM-RCM spread exceeds the parameter spread.
rows.notes: Model-based projection; future results cannot be validated but the model was checked against observations of the real system. Single method, one region and crop. Conclusion 1 frames results as conditional on a business-as-usual irrigation schedule, but this is an assumption, not a requirement stated from findings, so Q7 is no.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Supporting information tables S1-S4 are not included.
